claim: The bacterial RNAP σ subunit uses a wedge residue (an aromatic side chain) to invade the DNA duplex to stabilize the extrahelical conformation of a flipped-out base.
source: The bacterial RNAP σ subunit can be added to the list of proteins using a wedge residue (usually an aromatic side chain) to invade the DNA duplex to stabilize the extrahelical conformation of a flipped-out base (Lau et al., 1998; Davies et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2009; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript places the finding in context of other proteins with citations.

claim: Both aromatic residues (W256 and Y217) act in a context dependent manner—they are not important for the initial promoter binding step nor for binding the ss −10 element DNA.
source: The kinetic studies reveal that both aromatic residues (W256 and Y217) act in a context dependent manner—they are not important for the initial promoter binding step (Figure 5D) nor for binding the ss −10 element DNA (Figure 5E): instead W256 and Y217 act to increase the rate of the isomerization (promoter opening step) itself (Figure 5E,D), possibly by making contacts unique to the transition state that lower the energy barrier between RPi and RPo in the two-step kinetic scheme (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the kinetic findings with reference to figures.

claim: The W-dyad is universally conserved in housekeeping σ's (Gruber and Bryant, 1997).
